context_blurb:
A food chain is the path energy takes as one living thing eats another: grass to rabbit to fox. Nearly every chain on Earth starts with sunlight caught by plants; a few, at deep-sea vents and in some caves, run on chemical energy instead. Following that energy explains why hunters like foxes are always fewer than the animals they eat.

Ecologists number the feeding levels from the bottom. Producers, the plants and algae that make their own food, are the first level, and consumers, the eaters, stack above them. In a desert, a seed-eating mouse is a primary consumer, a snake that swallows it is a secondary consumer, and an owl that snatches the snake is a tertiary consumer, at the fourth level. An animal that hunted owls would make a fifth level, a quaternary consumer.

People are omnivores, eating both plants and animals, so a person can change levels from meal to meal. A hiker snacking on wild berries feeds as a primary consumer; dining later on a rabbit, which eats nothing but plants, he feeds one level higher, as a secondary consumer.

Little of the energy at one level reaches the next. A rabbit, like any warm-blooded animal, spends nearly all the energy it absorbs on living: moving, breathing, mending its body and keeping warm, and that energy ends up as heat given off to its surroundings. Less than a tenth is built into its body, the only part a fox can get. Feel the warmth of a sleeping dog: that is food energy leaving as heat.

Ecologists sum this up in the ten percent rule: roughly a tenth of one level's energy passes to the level above. So of the energy in a meadow's grass, a tenth reaches the rabbits and a tenth of that tenth reaches the foxes, about a hundredth, because the shares multiply at each step. The tenth is only a rough guide, since measured shares often run from about a twentieth to a fifth.

An energy pyramid draws the levels as stacked bars, each as wide as the energy it holds. Counting creatures instead can flip the picture: one oak may feed some two thousand leaf-eating insects, which feed far fewer birds, so a pyramid of numbers stands on its point. Measured by energy, though, the tree is the widest level, because every bit of energy the insects and birds get came from the oak, and most of it is spent and lost as heat at each step. A pyramid of energy is never upside down.

Each step up leaves less energy, so top predators are always far fewer than the plant-eaters below them. A bird that catches seed-eating mice feeds one level nearer the plants than a bird of the same size that catches frogs, which live on insects that live on plants; more energy is left for it, so a marsh can feed more of the mouse-catchers. Eating meat-eaters gives a hunter no extra energy; it only puts the hunter a level higher, where less is left.

Weight tells the same story: a songbird outweighs a grasshopper many times over, but a grassland holds so many more grasshoppers that all together they far outweigh the songbirds. What counts is the weight of the whole level, its biomass, not the size of one animal.

Wild food chains seldom pass four or five levels, because so much energy is spent and lost as heat at every step that too little energy is left for another level. That energy is not destroyed; it has become heat, which no living thing can use as food. Matter is different: the atoms in food return to the soil, water and air for plants to use again, so matter cycles while energy flows through and out. Energy is the textbook reason chains stay short, but not the whole story: a study of lakes, from small ponds up to Lake Erie, found longer chains in bigger lakes.

Decomposers, mainly fungi and bacteria, break down dead things. They feed on dead plants, droppings and dead animals from every level, top predators included, so they fit no single step, and ecologists usually leave them out of the count. They still take in a huge share of the energy: on land most plant growth is never eaten by plant-eaters while it lives, and the decomposers break it down when it dies. Tiny soil animals, such as springtails, feed on the decomposers in turn.
